key_terms.meaning: A converter system that holds a battery on a DC bus between a charger and an inverter so the load keeps running when the mains fails.
Rectifier charges the DC bus and the inverter always feeds the load, so the load never sees a mains dip; efficiency is lower than offline types.
Back-to-back thyristor pair that moves the load from the failed mains to the inverter output in a few milliseconds, with no moving parts.
t = (Ah × V × efficiency) ÷ load power, the time a battery can hold the load before its terminal voltage falls to the cut-off value.
Charger first holds a constant current until the battery reaches its gassing voltage, then holds a constant, slightly lower voltage while current tapers.
Delaying the TRIAC/SCR turn-on in each half cycle of the AC wave to set the RMS voltage fed to a lamp or heater.
Copper coil carrying the high-frequency current that induces the heating current inside the metal workpiece placed near it.
δ = √(ρ ÷ (π f μ)), depth below the surface where current density falls to 1/e; higher frequency f gives a thinner hot layer.
Power dissipated as heat by circulating currents induced in the body of the workpiece, the main heating mechanism above the Curie temperature.
Inverter with a capacitor in series with the work coil, driven near resonance so the coil current is large and the switching loss is small.
End station of an HVDC link holding the converter transformers, valve hall and filters that turn AC into DC or DC back into AC.

key_terms.term: Firing angle α and extinction angle γ
key_terms.meaning: α sets when a valve starts conducting and γ is the margin left before the voltage reverses; γ must stay positive for successful commutation.
Capacitance current of an AC cable or long line that flows even at no load; it is absent on a DC line, which is why HVDC suits long cables.
Shunt device that varies its reactive output continuously by thyristor switching of reactors and capacitors, holding bus voltage nearly constant.
Fixed reactor in series with a thyristor pair; delaying the firing angle reduces the current and so the reactive absorption.
Voltage-source inverter connected through a reactor; it exchanges reactive current by making its output voltage larger or smaller than the bus voltage.
Power converter that synchronises its output current with the grid voltage and pushes power from a DC source into the AC network.
Current controller that switches when the actual current crosses a band of width ±h around the reference, giving fast, robust but variable-frequency operation.
Control that continuously adjusts the DC operating voltage so that a solar array delivers its maximum available power.
Set point is the wanted value of the controlled variable; error e = set point − measured value drives the controller output.
The final device that acts on the process, here a power converter or thyristor switch controlling heater or motor power.

takeaways: A UPS is a charger, a battery and an inverter on a shared DC bus; the topology chosen decides efficiency, transfer time and cost.
A battery charger is a controlled DC source following a fixed current-then-voltage profile, and the same thyristor switching runs dimmers, timers and emergency lamps.
Induction heating puts the heat source inside the workpiece, so it is fast, clean and controllable by frequency and coil current.
HVDC carries bulk power without line charging current, has no stability limit over distance and gives full, fast control of power flow.
Thyristor-switched reactors and capacitors in SVC and FACTS devices hold voltage and push a line closer to its thermal limit without building new lines.
A grid-tied converter with a fast current loop fixes power factor, limits harmonics and lets power flow in either direction between DC source and grid.
Hysteresis current control is popular for grid interfaces because it is simple and robust, at the cost of variable switching frequency and wider ripple.
Every process-control loop is sensor, transmitter, controller and actuator; the actuator here is a power converter whose duty or firing angle is set by the error.
Small-signal sizing rules matter in practice: battery Ah for backup time, inverter kVA for surge load, PV kWp for daily energy, HVDC rating for bulk transfer.
bank_note: Long answers usually combine one block diagram with waveforms: draw the power circuit, mark the controlled switch and its firing instants, then explain how the output quantity (voltage, current, temperature, level) is held at the required value.

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of an online (double-conversion) UPS and explain the function of each block from mains input to load.
outline: Input filter and rectifier/charger feeding the DC bus
Battery bank floating on the DC bus with cut-off and protection
Inverter (usually PWM, IGBT) producing a clean sine at 50 Hz
Static bypass/transfer switch and its transfer time
Operation on mains, on failure, and on bypass; why the load never sees a dip

bank.q: Explain the constant-current then constant-voltage charging profile of a lead-acid battery and describe a thyristor-controlled charger that produces it.
outline: Why deep discharge needs current limit; gassing voltage at the CV point
CC phase: current held, terminal voltage rises
CV phase: voltage clamped, current tapers to float value
Thyristor bridge with phase control and current/voltage feedback
Need for ripple filtering and temperature compensation

bank.q: Explain the principle of induction heating and state why the heat is generated inside the workpiece rather than in the coil.
outline: Alternating current in the work coil creates an alternating magnetic field
Eddy currents in the conducting workpiece dissipate I²R heat
Hysteresis loss adds heat in magnetic workpieces below Curie temperature
Skin effect confines current to a thin surface layer
Why the coil stays comparatively cool; role of frequency and coupling

bank.q: Explain HVDC transmission with a two-terminal block diagram and list its advantages over EHV AC transmission.
outline: AC to DC converter stations at both ends, DC line, filters and control
Twelve-pulse or higher converter for low harmonics
No charging current, no Ferranti rise on cables
No stability limit on line length; asynchronous interconnection possible
Fast control of power by firing angle; cost break-even distance

bank.q: A home needs 600 W of backup for 4 hours from a 24 V battery bank. Find the Ah rating and the inverter kVA, allowing 85 percent inverter efficiency and 80 percent depth of discharge.
outline: Energy required = 600 × 4 = 2400 Wh
Battery energy = 2400 ÷ 0.85 ≈ 2823 Wh
Ah = 2823 ÷ 24 ≈ 118 Ah at full discharge
Divide by 0.8 depth of discharge gives about 147 Ah, choose 150 Ah
Inverter rating from load power and starting surge of motor loads

bank.q: A 230 V, 50 Hz mains feeds a lamp through a TRIAC with phase-angle control. Explain the firing circuit and describe how the RMS lamp voltage and power change as the firing angle is varied.
outline: DIAC-TRIAC triggering, RC charging of the timing capacitor each half cycle
Conduction from firing angle to the end of the half cycle
RMS output V = Vm√[(π−α)/2π + sin 2α/4π]-type relation
Brightness and power fall as α is delayed towards 180°
Snubber, dV/dt and radio-interference filtering

bank.q: Explain how an SVC built from a TCR and a fixed capacitor holds bus voltage, and show how the reactive output depends on the TCR firing angle.
outline: Fixed capacitor gives leading VARs, TCR gives lagging VARs
TCR current falls as firing angle moves from 90° to 180°
SVC susceptance B(α) is continuously variable between limits
Voltage regulator measures bus voltage and sets firing angle
Improvement of transfer capability and damping of oscillations

bank.q: Describe hysteresis current control for a single-phase grid-tied inverter. Explain switching logic, band width, and the resulting advantages and disadvantages.
outline: Reference current from power/FACTS command, synchronised with grid
Switch ON when actual current falls below lower band, OFF above upper band
Switching frequency depends on the slope of the current and the band
Advantages: fast, robust, simple, no tuning
Disadvantages: variable frequency, wide ripple spectrum, need for adaptive band or fixed-frequency variants

bank.q: Explain closed-loop temperature control of a furnace using a thyristor power controller, naming every element of the loop.
outline: Thermocouple sensor and transmitter producing a standard signal
Comparison with set point giving error
Controller (usually PID or ON-OFF) computing the output
Actuator: thyristor or SCR phase-angle/zero-crossing power controller
Process, disturbance handling, sensor lag and anti-windup

bank.q: Explain liquid level control of a tank using a power electronic actuator, and state what changes if the pump is fed by a variable-frequency drive.
outline: Float or pressure or ultrasonic sensor, transmitter and set point
Error drives pump voltage/frequency through the converter
Continuous (PID) versus ON-OFF control of the pump
VFD gives quadratic pump power saving versus throttling
Pump law P ∝ N³, protection against dry running and surge

bank.q: Compare offline, line-interactive and online UPS topologies for transfer time, efficiency, output quality and cost, and recommend one for a small office and one for a hospital theatre.
outline: Offline: load on mains, transfer in milliseconds, cheapest, poorest protection
Line-interactive: booster/buck tap or ferroresonant control, wider input window
Online: double conversion, zero transfer time, best waveform, lowest efficiency
Power factor, crest factor and overload capability of loads
Justified choice with reasoning for both cases

bank.q: Explain why conventional diode-bridge front ends draw distorted current, and describe how unity-power-factor rectification and an active harmonic filter correct it.
outline: Non-sinusoidal pulsed current, high THD, low power factor at the source
Active front end with hysteresis or PWM current control on the AC side
Reference current from a template of the supply voltage, unity power factor
Active harmonic filter injects the harmonic component in antiphase
Limits of standards, filter inductor and bandwidth, effect on DC bus

bank.q: A state utility must move 1500 MW over a long distance and also needs voltage support on a weak bus. Evaluate the choice between an HVDC link and an AC line with an SVC.
outline: HVDC: no charging current, no distance stability limit, asynchronous link, cost break-even
AC line with SVC: reactive support, better voltage, higher transfer limit, cheaper at short distance
Losses, converter harmonics and filters, protection complexity
Controllability and speed of response; black start and multi-terminal options
Justified recommendation

bank.q: Evaluate induction heating against resistance heating for a domestic cooking plate and for surface hardening of a steel gear.
outline: Heat source inside the workpiece versus outside; coupling needs ferromagnetic or well-conducting pan
Thermal efficiency, warm-up time, cleanliness and safety
Hardening needs thin skin depth, so high frequency; power supply cost
Coil design, resonant inverter topology, power factor correction
Conclusion per application

glossary.def: Any power electronic circuit that changes the form of electric power: AC to DC, DC to AC, DC to DC or AC to AC.
A converter that turns DC into AC, usually by switching devices in a bridge and shaping the output with PWM.
A converter that turns AC into DC; diode rectifiers are uncontrolled, thyristor rectifiers have a controllable output.
Four-layer latching switch that conducts only after a gate pulse and turns off only when its current falls below the holding value.
Bidirectional thyristor that conducts in both half cycles, which makes it the standard switch in lamp dimmers and small AC controllers.
Bidirectional trigger diode that breaks over at a fixed voltage and is used to fire a TRIAC in a simple RC phase-shift circuit.
Insulated gate bipolar transistor; voltage-controlled switch combining MOS gate drive with low ON-state drop, widely used in inverters and drives.
Pulse-width modulation: switching on and off at a fixed frequency and varying the on-time to synthesise a wanted average voltage.
D = Ton ÷ T, the fraction of the switching period a device conducts; it sets the output of DC-DC converters and the fundamental of inverters.
PF = P ÷ S, the ratio of real power to apparent power; it falls when current is out of phase with voltage or rich in harmonics.
THD = √(Σ Vn²) ÷ V1 over n ≥ 2, the ratio of all harmonic content to the fundamental, in per cent.
Q = V I sin φ, the power that oscillates between source and reactive element, in var or kvar; it loads the line without doing real work.
Diode placed across an inductive load to carry the stored current when the main switch turns off, protecting the switch and improving output.
Small RC or RCD network across a switching device that limits dV/dt and absorbs turn-off energy.
The process of transferring current from one device or phase to another; in line-commutated converters the supply voltage itself forces turn-off.
Condition where a grid-connected inverter keeps feeding a local network after the grid has tripped; anti-islanding protection must detect and stop it.
Battery energy storage system: a battery bank with a bidirectional converter that can both charge from and discharge into the grid.
A shunt converter that senses the load current, extracts its harmonic content and injects an equal and opposite current to clean the supply.
Thyristor controlled series capacitor: a thyristor-controlled reactor in parallel with a series capacitor, giving a variable series reactance in the line.
Flexible AC transmission system: power electronic controllers, shunt or series, that make an AC network controllable and raise its usable capacity.
Circuit that converts a sensor output into a standard signal, such as 4–20 mA or 1–5 V, for the controller.
Control law with proportional, integral and derivative terms on the error; it holds the process variable at the set point despite disturbances.
Turning a thyristor on only at the instant the supply voltage crosses zero, used for heaters to avoid the harmonics of phase control.
The unwanted AC component left on a DC voltage or current after rectification, usually reduced by filters or higher switching frequency.
